clusters.name: Monitoring Evidence Modality
clusters.description: The observable evidence used to assess deployed-agent behavior, including rewards, outputs, reasoning, actions, telemetry, internal state, and human judgments.

values.label: Continuous output evaluation
values.description: Ongoing assessment of deployed outputs for performance decay, quality drift, and behavioral change.

values.label: Human output-quality review
values.description: Periodic human scoring of production outputs for relevance, correctness, trustworthiness, or subtle drift.

values.label: Model-confidence monitoring
values.description: Using confidence scores as an RL-specific signal for deployed behavior and inference quality.

values.label: Infrastructure-health telemetry
values.description: Monitoring CPU, memory, network, latency, and related infrastructure signals alongside agent behavior.

values.label: Reward-signal monitoring
values.description: Monitoring scalar or proxy rewards as evidence of agent performance.

values.label: Proxy-reward monitoring
values.description: Monitoring proxy rewards that may diverge from real-world or true task outcomes.

values.label: Behavior-trace diagnostics
values.description: Analyzing actions, trajectories, outputs, tool traces, and logs.

values.label: Chain-of-thought monitoring
values.description: Using reasoning traces to inspect exploits, misalignment, or concealed intent.

values.label: Action-only monitoring
values.description: Monitoring externally visible actions without access to reasoning traces.

values.label: Operational service telemetry
values.description: Using latency, errors, resource use, feature availability, and invocation signals.

values.label: Human-oracle scoring
values.description: Using human judgments as evidence alongside automated evaluation.

values.label: External-world feedback
values.description: Using real-world outcomes rather than only internal reward or evaluator signals.

values.label: Activation-state monitoring
values.description: Monitoring internal activations, values, entropy, weights, or related model state.

values.label: Scratchpad reasoning observability
values.description: Using exposed scratchpad or hidden-reasoning traces to inspect belief use, evaluation awareness, alignment faking, or reward-hacking intent.

values.label: Automated safety-flag signals
values.description: Using classifiers or keyword detectors to flag harmful, biased, or inappropriate outputs at production scale.

values.label: Exploration-pattern monitoring
values.description: Monitoring exploration behavior to identify unsafe, anomalous, or unusually risky production actions.

values.label: System-health telemetry
values.description: Monitoring infrastructure and service-health signals alongside agent behavior and reward signals.

values.label: User-behavior feedback signals
values.description: Using rephrasing, edits, clarifications, bounce rates, usage, and related user behavior as indirect evidence of agent quality or drift.

values.label: Activation-delta monitoring
values.description: Monitoring changes in internal activations between clean and drifted inputs.

values.label: Observation-signal monitoring
values.description: Monitoring environment observations and externally visible state.

values.label: Agent-state monitoring
values.description: Monitoring internal state, values, entropy, activations, or weights.

values.label: Chain-of-thought monitoring signal
values.description: Using generated reasoning traces as monitoring evidence.

values.label: Chain-of-thought misalignment monitoring
values.description: Using reasoning traces to inspect misalignment or cheating.

clusters.name: Detection Target
clusters.description: The production failure or change that monitoring infrastructure is intended to identify.

values.label: Deployment-resilience failure
values.description: Failure to remain safe and effective under changing real-world deployment conditions despite training-time compliance.

values.label: Ethical-drift detection
values.description: Detecting drift toward unfair, toxic, biased, or otherwise ethically unacceptable behavior.

values.label: Behavioral phase-transition detection
values.description: Detecting abrupt qualitative behavioral changes associated with increased optimization capability or distribution change.

values.label: Distribution-drift detection
values.description: Detecting changes in input, concept, model, or live feature distributions.

values.label: Novel-situation detection
values.description: Detecting unfamiliar situations while distinguishing harmless novelty from capability-relevant hazards.

values.label: Capability-boundary detection
values.description: Detecting situations beyond the agent's reliable capabilities.

values.label: Reward-behavior divergence detection
values.description: Detecting high or improving reward paired with poor intended-task performance.

values.label: Alignment-faking detection
values.description: Detecting apparently compliant behavior that conceals a different objective or harmful intent.

values.label: False-negative-rate detection
values.description: Detecting missed harmful or emerging behavior through production error-rate monitoring.

values.label: Subtle-cheating detection gap
values.description: Failure to detect increasingly sophisticated or concealed cheating.

values.label: Intent-concealment outcome
values.description: The agent hides misaligned intent or behavior in response to monitoring or penalties.

clusters.name: Detection Method
clusters.description: The statistical, learned, comparative, or rule-based mechanism used to identify the selected production failure.

values.label: BFAR degradation test
values.description: A BFAR-based test for detecting reward degradation after environmental change without retraining.

values.label: Embedding-cluster comparison
values.description: Comparing proportions of baseline and later embedding clusters to detect semantic input shifts.

values.label: CUSUM degradation test
values.description: A sequential CUSUM test considered as an alternative for detecting degradation.

values.label: Hotelling mean-shift test
values.description: A multivariate Hotelling test considered as an alternative for detecting reward degradation.

values.label: Naive mean degradation test
values.description: A simple-mean test considered as a conventional but non-adopted degradation detector.

values.label: Statistical drift testing
values.description: Using KL divergence, MMD, empirical distributions, drift indices, or related statistical tests.

values.label: LLM-based behavioral monitoring
values.description: Using a separate language model to inspect reasoning or behavior for exploits and misalignment.

values.label: Reward-model ensemble detection
values.description: Using multiple reward models and disagreement or agreement requirements to identify gaming.

values.label: Normal safety evaluation
values.description: Using ordinary safety evaluations to detect readily observable harmful behavior.

values.label: Detection incompleteness
values.description: Partial detector coverage leaves some anomalous or reward-hacking behavior unobserved.

relations.rationale: Detection methods operationalize the selected detection target.

clusters.name: Evaluation Test Strategy
clusters.description: The environments, timing, adversarial procedures, and comparison methods used to validate deployed-agent behavior.

values.label: Periodic benchmark evaluation
values.description: Running task-appropriate benchmarks at intervals to detect performance degradation.

values.label: Fixed-query regression evaluation
values.description: Repeatedly evaluating a fixed query set and comparing results with historical performance.

values.label: Cross-architecture validation
values.description: Validating reward and monitoring improvements across model architectures to detect architecture-specific effects.

values.label: Trap-based adversarial validation
values.description: Using traps, trip-wires, and adversarial training cases to expose shortcut discovery and superficial hacking.

values.label: Held-out environment evaluation

iterations.explanation:
Merged near-duplicate dimensions (33 -> 24):
  - "Monitoring Evidence Modality" + "Monitoring Signal Types" → "Monitoring Evidence Modality"
  - "Anomaly and Drift Detection" + "Detection Method" → "Anomaly and Drift Detection"
  - "Evaluation and Test Strategy" + "Evaluation Test Strategy" → "Evaluation and Test Strategy"
  - "Update Execution Strategy" + "Feedback and Update Strategy" → "Update Execution Strategy"
  - "Runtime Safety Intervention" + "Safe Action Intervention" + "Safe Action Intervention Strategy" → "Runtime Safety Intervention"
  - "Monitoring Aggregation Strategy" + "Monitoring Aggregation Cadence" → "Monitoring Aggregation Strategy"
  - "Reward Objective Representation" + "Reward Representation Strategy" → "Reward Objective Representation"
  - "Release Rollback Strategy" + "Release and Rollback Strategy" → "Release Rollback Strategy"
Consolidated 525 draft values across 24 dimensions (merge threshold 0.350, borderline band 0.400). Merged 36 near-duplicate values:
  - [Monitoring Evidence Modality] "System-health telemetry" → "Infrastructure-health telemetry"
  - [Monitoring Evidence Modality] "Chain-of-thought monitoring", "Chain-of-thought misalignment monitoring" → "Chain-of-Thought monitoring for misaligned behavior"
  - [Monitoring Evidence Modality] "Agent-state monitoring" → "Activation-state monitoring"
  - [Monitoring Evidence Modality] "Action-only reward-hack monitoring" → "Action-only monitoring"
  - [Evaluation and Test Strategy] "Held-out environment evaluation" → "Behavior evaluation in held-out scenarios"
  - [Evaluation and Test Strategy] "Adversarial reward testing" → "Adversarial reward-hacking evaluation"

values.label: Model-confidence monitoring

values.label: Reward-signal monitoring

values.label: Proxy-reward monitoring

values.label: Behavior-trace diagnostics

values.label: Chain-of-Thought monitoring for misaligned behavior
values.description: Monitoring reasoning traces for misalignment or cheating.

clusters.name: Detection Target

values.label: Distribution-drift detection

values.label: Novel-situation detection
values.description: Detecting unfamiliar situations while distinguishing harmless novelty from capability-relevant hazards.

values.label: Reward-behavior divergence detection

values.label: Alignment-faking detection

values.label: False-negative-rate detection

values.label: Behavioral phase-transition detection

values.label: Subtle-cheating detection gap

values.label: Intent-concealment outcome

values.label: Empirical-CDF distribution monitoring

values.label: Anomaly detection
values.description: Detection of unusual behavior or reward exploitation.

values.label: Output-pattern anomaly detection
values.description: Detection of suspicious output patterns.

values.label: KL-divergence monitoring
values.description: Policy divergence measured with KL divergence.

values.label: Data-drift monitoring
values.description: Input distribution monitoring.

values.label: Concept-drift monitoring
values.description: Input-output relationship monitoring.

values.label: Model-drift monitoring
values.description: Monitoring changing production behavior.

values.label: Novelty detection
values.description: Detection of unfamiliar scenarios.

values.label: Capability-relevant unknown detection

values.label: Scenario-based OOD definition

values.label: Metric-divergence alerting

values.label: Hallucination-rate monitoring
values.description: Invalid-claim rate monitoring.

values.label: Bias-score monitoring
values.description: Demographic or customer bias monitoring.

values.label: Accuracy-drift monitoring
values.description: Accuracy monitoring over time.

values.label: Threshold KPI alerting
values.description: Alerts on KPI thresholds.

values.label: BFAR degradation test
values.description: A BFAR-based test for detecting reward degradation after environmental change without retraining.

values.label: Embedding-cluster comparison
values.description: Comparing proportions of baseline and later embedding clusters to detect semantic input shifts.

values.label: CUSUM degradation test
values.description: A sequential CUSUM test considered as an alternative for detecting degradation.

values.label: Hotelling mean-shift test
values.description: A multivariate Hotelling test considered as an alternative for detecting reward degradation.

values.label: Naive mean degradation test
values.description: A simple-mean test considered as a conventional but non-adopted degradation detector.

values.label: Statistical drift testing
values.description: Using KL divergence, MMD, empirical distributions, drift indices, or related statistical tests.

values.label: LLM-based behavioral monitoring
values.description: Using a separate language model to inspect reasoning or behavior for exploits and misalignment.

values.label: Reward-model ensemble detection
values.description: Using multiple reward models and disagreement or agreement requirements to identify gaming.

values.label: Normal safety evaluation
values.description: Using ordinary safety evaluations to detect readily observable harmful behavior.

values.label: Perplexity drift indicator
values.description: Using increased perplexity on recent text as an indicator of language-model drift.

values.label: Human-rated quality decline
values.description: A declining trend in human relevance and correctness ratings as evidence of production drift.

values.label: Explicit edge-case testing

values.label: Simulator-to-reality validation

values.label: Offline-live correlation checks

values.label: Adversarial policy evaluation
values.description: Opponent policies expose hidden vulnerabilities.

values.label: Proxy-true reward correlation

values.label: Runtime OOD evaluation

values.label: Unseen-regime stress testing

values.label: Continuous post-deployment evaluation
values.description: Evaluation continues after ownership and deployment.

values.label: Output-equality correctness criterion

values.label: No-op optimized implementation

values.label: Diverse scenario evaluation

values.description: Combining rule-based and model-based reward checks.

saturation_history.rationale: Not tested: the taxonomy was generated from this minibatch.

The taxonomy covers the main choices about which signals to monitor, how oversight is allocated, how policies are updated, and how incidents are contained. However, several relevant architectural choices are not subsumed by those dimensions. First, the taxonomy lacks a diagnostic-processing dimension covering when diagnostics are computed, their temporal window and cadence, whether they are sliced by interaction mode, and how statistics are aggregated across distributed workers. These are distinct from selecting monitoring signals. Second, it lacks a reference-based behavioral-comparison dimension covering comparison with a trusted baseline, repeated-rollout action-distribution analysis, and the choice of statistical distance such as Jensen–Shannon divergence or Hellinger distance. Third, production RL infrastructure concerns involving environment modeling and safe exploration are not captured by the current hosting, release, or incident-containment dimensions. Other codes describe forces, outcomes, specific detector implementations, feedback mechanisms, or policy-update options already absorbable by the existing dimensions.

uncovered_concepts: Runtime shield between policy and environment
Static shielding based on fixed dynamics and hazard boundaries
saturation_history.rationale: Most codes are covered by existing dimensions: signal selection and detector design cover Chain-of-Thought, drift, novelty, tail, bias, hallucination, and reward-hacking monitoring; reward representation and verification cover proxy audits, reward shaping, multi-objective evaluation, and adversarial testing; update execution and feedback dimensions cover retraining, fine-tuning, continual learning, domain adaptation, retrieval/editing, and human feedback; and incident evidence, containment, and release/rollback dimensions cover shadow runs, canaries, fallbacks, rollback actions, alerting, and postmortems. However, the minibatch reveals three architectural axes not adequately represented. First, it introduces runtime input and telemetry fault handling—schema validation, fail-fast ingestion, defaults, and degrade-safe behavior—which is distinct from incident containment after a failure. Second, it distinguishes rollback actions from the policy that selects rollback triggers and their automation, including quality, error, latency, drift, resource, and manual triggers. Third, it introduces runtime action mediation between the policy and environment: whether to block or replace unsafe actions, how static versus adaptive shields are designed, how shield interventions are monitored under shift, and how unknown situations produce alerts or human handoff. These concepts are directly relevant to post-deployment RL monitoring architecture and cannot be added to existing dimensions without conflating distinct decisions.

uncovered_concepts: Offline reinforcement learning for constrained environments
Online or hybrid learning for safe experimentation
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes through existing dimensions for reward verification, monitoring combinations, update execution, release and rollback, feedback reuse, drift monitoring, and safe action intervention. However, several relevant architectural choices are not fully subsumed. First, adversarial policy evaluation introduces a distinct robustness-testing axis: whether and how deployed policies are challenged by intentionally trained adversaries, including whether discovered attacks are addressed through adversarial fine-tuning. Existing adversarial reward-function testing focuses on the reward specification rather than policy-level attack generation and robustness. Second, offline versus online or hybrid learning is a distinct interaction-regime decision driven by safety, experimentation cost, data availability, and legal constraints; the update dimension covers update timing and placement but does not clearly represent this axis. Third, sandboxed agent isolation is an execution-boundary decision that prevents agents from manipulating reward or evaluation mechanisms, rather than merely detecting or blocking unsafe actions. Finally, API gateways, request rate limiting, and authentication/authorization represent an inference-interface protection decision involving access control and capacity protection. These concerns are only indirectly implied by hosting and containment dimensions and cannot be absorbed without conflating hosting with interface security and traffic-control policy.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: reward and proxy design by Reward Representation Strategy and Reward Verification Strategy; evaluator, oracle, human, and multi-channel feedback arrangements by Oversight Allocation Strategy, Feedback Acquisition Strategy, and Monitoring Combination Strategy; telemetry, drift, anomaly, and statistical testing by Monitoring Signal Types and Monitoring Combination Strategy; and deployment, updating, rollback, canary, shadow, safety filtering, and intervention mechanisms by the corresponding deployment, update, release, containment, and safe-action dimensions. The model/runtime ownership split is a distinct architectural governance decision assigning accountability between model-development and production-runtime teams. Existing dimensions include human oversight and incident runbooks, but do not capture alternative organizational ownership or responsibility-allocation arrangements, so this concept is not fully subsumed.

uncovered_concepts: Model quantization for inference resource reduction
Knowledge distillation for inference resource reduction
saturation_history.rationale: Most codes are subsumed by existing dimensions for monitoring evidence, signal composition and cadence, anomaly/drift detection, reward verification, evaluation, feedback, rollback, intervention, and hosting. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct decision axis for the temporal/staged architecture of optimization: whether agents optimize environment rewards and human approval sequentially or jointly, and how much multi-step lookahead is permitted. This is not merely reward representation, oversight allocation, or update cadence; it changes the optimization architecture and the exposure to multi-step reward hacking. The taxonomy also lacks a distinct inference-resource optimization decision covering model compression and serving execution choices such as quantization, distillation, and request batching. These choices trade off latency, throughput, cost, and alignment or safety quality and are not equivalent to selecting a hosting foundation. Other related codes describe risks, outcomes, or implementation-specific instances that can be absorbed into these axes or existing monitoring and containment dimensions.

uncovered_concepts: Alert deduplication by policy and deployment
Federated offline RL for privacy-sensitive logs
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: feedback-source alternatives by Feedback Acquisition Strategy and Oversight Allocation Strategy; monitoring placement and in-loop diagnostics by Monitoring Combination Strategy and Update Execution Strategy; offline policy evaluation by Evaluation and Test Strategy; logging, provenance, dashboards, and data-quality checks by Incident Evidence Strategy; rollout and shadow/canary patterns by Deployment Exposure Strategy; and reward-hacking, evaluator, and integrity concerns by Reward Verification Strategy and Anomaly and Drift Detection. The alert-routing, deduplication, and cooldown codes reveal an uncovered operational decision axis concerning alert lifecycle and notification management, distinct from what is being monitored, how evidence is aggregated, and what triggers rollback. Federated offline RL reveals an uncovered training-data/computation-topology decision—centralized versus federated placement under privacy constraints—which is not captured by the existing offline/online update or hosting dimensions.

All relevant open codes are subsumed by existing taxonomy dimensions. Prompt-based and other reward-hacking mitigations fit Reward Verification Strategy, Reward Objective/Transformation Strategy, and existing reward-hacking mitigation values. Edge deployment, compact policies, federated and offline RL, simulation, replay, counterfactual evaluation, and service-level objectives fit Deployment Hosting, Update Execution, Evaluation and Test, Monitoring Evidence, and Monitoring Aggregation dimensions. Alert prioritization, learned filtering, human validation, continuous monitoring, and cross-functional assessment fit Incident Evidence, Oversight Allocation, Monitoring Signal/Combination, and Feedback Acquisition dimensions. Artifact registries, lineage, data lakes, telemetry capture, storage formats, access controls, and audit mechanisms fit Incident Evidence Strategy and Deployment Hosting Strategy. Threshold qualification, traffic shifting, registry-pointer changes, configuration-based rollback, and automated rollback workflows fit Rollback Trigger, Rollback Recovery, and Release and Rollback Strategy. Human feedback protocols, annotator training, complex-case workflows, and feedback-resource constraints fit Feedback Acquisition and Oversight Allocation. The remaining codes describe outcomes, risks, forces, or implementation details rather than genuinely new architectural decision axes.

The taxonomy is theoretically saturated for this minibatch. The open codes are either directly represented or can be absorbed by existing axes: reward and process-signal design, consistency and rubric-based verification, adversarial/trap testing, cross-architecture and distribution-shift evaluation, sequential and episodic degradation detection, false-alarm and statistically significant alerting, continuous output and human review, retraining/fine-tuning/continual-learning/retrieval update strategies, feedback and annotation workflows, evaluator and reward-model risks, reward-hacking outcomes, infrastructure and RL-specific telemetry, hosting scalability and redundancy, access control and artifact security, runtime circuit breakers and fallback policies, and monitoring aggregation. Several codes describe forces, risks, outcomes, examples, or implementation tools rather than distinct architectural decisions; these do not require new dimensions. Open release of artifacts is outside the stated post-deployment monitoring infrastructure design space. Concepts such as BFAR, CUSUM, Hotelling tests, ESS, tail metrics, and KL caps are specific alternatives or controls within existing detection, aggregation, and intervention dimensions rather than new axes.

dropped_dimensions.rationale: Dropped because reward-objective representation is primarily a training and reward-design decision. Although it influences what monitoring should observe, classifying documents by reward structure does not directly describe the architecture of post-deployment monitoring infrastructure.

Dropped because reward transformation concerns reward shaping, normalization, clipping, and penalty design during learning. These are upstream training-time choices rather than alternative architectures for monitoring a deployed agent.

Dropped because feedback reuse describes how feedback is propagated into later training, fine-tuning, or adaptation. That is a downstream model-improvement activity, not the monitoring infrastructure used to observe deployed behavior.

Dropped because update execution strategy primarily concerns retraining, online learning, fine-tuning, and model-update orchestration. These may consume monitoring outputs, but they are outside the use case's focus on architectural decisions for post-deployment monitoring infrastructure.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains extensive overlap between dimensions. Merge 27 (Monitoring Signal Composition) with 31 (Monitoring Combination Strategy), since both ask how monitoring signals and detectors are combined. Merge 16 (Incident Evidence Strategy) with 23 (Incident Evidence Management), whose questions and values both cover capturing, validating, storing, routing, and using incident evidence. Merge 5 (Reward Verification Architecture) with 15 (Reward Verification Strategy), which both ask how reward and evaluator integrity are verified. Keep 20 (Rollback Trigger Strategy) separate from 22 (Release Rollback Strategy), but move trigger values such as 22.16–22.19 to 20 so 22 focuses on release exposure and rollback mechanisms. These repeated questions substantially reduce dimensional distinctness, although dimensions such as 2 (Detection Target) and 13 (Anomaly and Drift Detection) ask different questions and should remain separate.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions have informative names and value descriptions, and statuses generally identify alternatives versus outcomes. However, several dimensions and values are difficult to distinguish. Dimension 1, "Monitoring Evidence Modality," mixes evidence types, evaluation procedures, and outcomes; merge duplicates such as 1.2/1.10, 1.4/1.9, and 1.8/1.13/1.19, and move outcome values 1.20 and 1.21 out of the candidate alternatives. Dimensions 27, "Monitoring Signal Composition," and 31, "Monitoring Combination Strategy," have near-identical questions and overlapping values; merge them and move cadence/granularity options such as 31.4-31.6 to dimension 9. Dimensions 16, "Incident Evidence Strategy," and 23, "Incident Evidence Management," likewise describe nearly the same evidence-management decision; merge them and remove or consolidate duplicated dashboard, logging, provenance, and data-capture values. Dimension 13, "Anomaly and Drift Detection," contains overlapping alternatives such as 13.6/13.12, 13.9/13.10, and 13.15/13.16, plus outcomes 13.32-13.37; consolidate equivalent detector labels and separate those outcomes from detector choices. Dimensions 20, "Rollback Trigger Strategy," and 22, "Release Rollback Strategy," repeat options such as automated rollback, manual rollback, and threshold triggers; merge the repeated values or move trigger-specific values consistently into one dimension.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the main post-deployment RL monitoring decision areas with multiple candidate options: evidence selection (1), detection targets (2), anomaly and drift detectors (13), signal combination and aggregation (31, 27, 9), incident evidence capture and management (16, 23), oversight (12), reward verification (5, 15), runtime intervention (8), rollback and recovery (20, 22, 26), deployment exposure (25), evaluation (14), and feedback acquisition (17). Each of these dimensions has several accepted, rejected, or mixed alternatives, so no major use-case area is left without a decision point. The main revision opportunity is organizational rather than coverage-related: dimensions 27 and 25 are comparatively narrow, but they still contain multiple candidates and therefore satisfy the stated criterion; no concrete coverage shortcoming is evident.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions directly fit post-deployment monitoring infrastructure, especially 1 Monitoring Evidence Modality, 2 Detection Target, 9 Monitoring Aggregation Strategy, 13 Anomaly and Drift Detection, 16 Incident Evidence Strategy, 23 Incident Evidence Management, and 27 Monitoring Signal Composition. However, substantial content is outside the requested lifecycle and decision kind. Drop 7 Deployment Hosting Strategy, whose values concern serving topology, quantization, autoscaling, and endpoint deployment rather than monitoring. Split 14 Evaluation and Test Strategy into post-deployment evaluation and pre-deployment testing, retaining only existing values such as 14.17 Runtime OOD evaluation and 14.19 Continuous post-deployment evaluation in the former. Drop or merge 15 Reward Verification Strategy into 5 Reward Verification Architecture, since most values such as 15.1 χ² occupancy regularization and 15.2 Preference-as-reward modeling concern training-time reward design. Drop 25 Deployment Exposure Strategy, which addresses release sequencing rather than monitoring after deployment. Reorganize 22 Release Rollback Strategy so release-gate values such as 22.1 Shadow deployment and 22.2 Canary deployment are separated from post-incident rollback decisions already represented by 20 Rollback Trigger Strategy and 26 Rollback Recovery Strategy.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Several catch-all buckets remain. Drop value 13.9 "Anomaly detection" because its generic description duplicates the many specific detectors in dimension 13; drop value 15.17 "Robust reward-hacking mitigation solutions" because it bundles unspecified mitigations already represented by specific values; and drop value 16.9 "Observability dashboards" because dimensions 16 and 23 already contain concrete dashboard options. Dimensions 16 "Incident Evidence Strategy" and 23 "Incident Evidence Management" also act as broad evidence-management buckets spanning dashboards, provenance, routing, storage, and operations; merge them and reorganize their existing values under more focused content rather than retaining both broad containers.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The JSON format is present, but the taxonomy frequently violates the one-decision-per-dimension and option-versus-subtopic rules. Dimension 31, "Monitoring Combination Strategy," combines signal composition, granularity, cadence, and automation; split it into separate decision questions using its existing values. Dimensions 16, "Incident Evidence Strategy," and 23, "Incident Evidence Management," each bundle capture, storage, provenance, dashboards, routing, and response decisions; split each into narrower questions and redistribute their existing values. Dimension 7, "Deployment Hosting Strategy," similarly combines topology, scaling, model representation, security, and resource placement; split those decision points. In dimension 2, "Detection Target," move 2.8 "False-negative-rate detection" to dimension 13 because it is a detection method, and reclassify or move 2.9–2.11 as outcomes rather than target options. In dimension 14, "Evaluation and Test Strategy," move exploit examples such as 14.21 "Intermediate-memory reuse exploit" and 14.22 "No-op optimized implementation" to an existing outcome-oriented dimension instead of treating them as evaluation alternatives.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many dimensions with at least two candidates, but several dimensions combine different decision questions. Dimension 31, "Monitoring Combination Strategy," mixes signal composition, diagnostic granularity, cadence, detector selection, release gates, and deployment evaluation; move its aggregation/cadence values (31.4–31.6) to dimension 9, detector values to 13, and exposure/release values (31.21–31.23) to 22 or 25, then merge the remaining composition alternatives with 27. Dimension 7, "Deployment Hosting Strategy," combines topology, scaling, resource optimization, security, and latency measurement; split it into hosting topology, serving optimization, and deployment security questions, ensuring each retains at least two existing candidates. Dimensions 16 and 23 both mix evidence capture, storage, dashboards, routing, validation, and operational response; merge their overlapping evidence-management candidates after moving 16.8 to 8 or 28 and 16.18 to 17. Dimension 15, "Reward Verification Strategy," combines reward modeling, regularization, adversarial testing, integrity controls, and post-release discovery; split it into reward/evaluator integrity controls and reward-hacking testing/mitigation, with at least two existing candidates in each. Dimension 1, "Monitoring Evidence Modality," also mixes evidence types with review processes and infrastructure telemetry; move human-review alternatives to 12 and operational telemetry to 23 or 7, leaving the evidence-signal alternatives together.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy uses the allowed status values, and many genuine effects are correctly marked as outcomes, but there are substantial status/type violations. In dimension 1, values 1.20 Action-only monitoring and 1.21 Chain-of-thought monitoring signal are alternative monitoring modalities, not outcomes; relabel them as candidate decisions. In dimensions 2, 13, 31, and 12, 2.9 Behavioral phase-transition detection, 13.32 Perplexity drift indicator, 31.32 Automated gaming-behavior safeguards, 31.33 Reward-hacking detection classifiers, 31.34 Formal hackability analysis frameworks, and 12.13 Behavior-only monitoring are also candidate strategies or detection choices mislabeled as outcomes; relabel them as candidates. Conversely, 14.21 Intermediate-memory reuse exploit and 14.22 No-op optimized implementation describe exploitation effects but are marked accepted; mark them as outcomes. Several mixed values do not express disagreement: 1.5, 2.1, 8.14, 9.2, 14.9, 15.3, 15.17, 15.19, 17.22, and 26.3 should either explicitly state that sources disagree or be changed to accepted/rejected. Dimension 26 also contains the same safe-fallback decision under different statuses: 26.3 Safe fallback policy is mixed while 26.6 Safe-baseline rollback is accepted; merge or distinguish these values and give the shared decision one status.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under at least one taxonomy dimension. Examples include s19_p02 under explanation-assisted monitoring, reward-function integrity testing, simulation, staged rollout, drift monitoring, and rollback; s08_p03 under statistical and embedding-cluster drift detection; s07_p02 under duration-qualified triggers and traffic-shifting, registry-pointer, or configuration rollback; s18_p03 under tool-conditioned support-mismatch and tail monitoring; and s22_p07 under feedback acquisition and human oversight. The background passage s15_p01 is decision-irrelevant. No unplaceable decision-bearing passage or taxonomy revision is required.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many adopted options, including drift and embedding monitoring from s08_p03, rollback methods from s07_p02, BFAR and competing tests from s02_p04, CoT monitoring from s27_p03, A/B testing and inference logging from s20_p05, and deployment gateways, authentication, and rate limiting from s21_p01. However, it misses several specific options: add SHAP/counterfactual-policy explainability and regret-analysis monitoring to dimension 1, supported by s19_p02; add rule-based and model-based verifier alternatives to dimension 5, supported by s14_p04; add structured rubric rewards, gated reward accumulation, verbalization fine-tuning, and policy/reward co-optimization to dimension 15, supported by s14_p04; add reward redesign, reward clipping, and inoculation prompting to dimension 15, supported by s06_p18; and add explicit reward-hacking behaviors such as verbosity/length hacking, sycophancy, boilerplate, and keyword stuffing to the relevant reward-hacking outcome dimension, supported by s29_p07.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions relevant to post-deployment RL monitoring: signal choice (1), reward design (2), oversight responsibility (3), hosting (4), policy release (5), incident response (6), and feedback acquisition (7). The clearest overlap is between dimension 6, Incident Evidence and Containment, and dimension 5, Policy Update and Release Strategy: value 6.2, Canary threshold control, is a release-gating and traffic-rollout decision that answers dimension 5's question and should be moved there. The related values 5.4, Validation-gated deployment, and 5.6, Production policy A/B testing, reinforce this overlap. Do not merge dimensions 5 and 6, since rollback/release decisions and incident containment remain different questions.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions clearly state their decision scope and provide distinguishable value descriptions, such as the separate reward, observation, agent-state, and behavior-trace options in dimension 1. The main revision needed is dimension 4, "Deployment Hosting Strategy": value 4.5, "Distributed training infrastructure," concerns training rather than hosting or serving; rename the dimension and description to cover deployment and RL infrastructure, and sharpen 4.2 versus 4.3 to distinguish managed policy serving from an end-to-end managed RL platform. In dimension 2, values 2.1, "Scalar proxy reward," and 2.6, "Single-metric optimization," are difficult to distinguish; explicitly frame 2.1 as the reward objective and 2.6 as a single evaluation or monitoring metric. Dimension 5 also has some near-overlap between 5.3, "Continuous online updating," and 5.7, "Continuous policy deployment"; clarify that 5.3 changes the live policy through online learning while 5.7 releases separately versioned policies.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: No major coverage shortcoming is evident. The taxonomy represents the main post-deployment RL monitoring areas—signals (1.1–1.6), reward integrity (2.1–2.7), oversight (3.1–3.4), hosting (4.1–4.5), policy release (5.1–5.8), incident containment (6.1–6.7), and feedback collection (7.1–7.6)—and every dimension provides several candidate decisions with accepted or rejected statuses. This adequately covers the architectural decisions practitioners face in production monitoring infrastructure.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Dimensions 1, 3, and 6 are directly relevant: signal selection, oversight allocation, and incident evidence/containment are core decisions for post-deployment RL monitoring infrastructure. Dimension 7 is partly relevant through production experience-data collection (7.4) and replay-buffer rehearsal (7.5), but preference propagation (7.3) and comparative preference supervision (7.6) are mainly training concerns; move the monitoring-relevant values into dimension 6 or narrow the dimension accordingly. Dimension 2, Reward Integrity Strategy, focuses largely on reward-objective design and training safeguards rather than monitoring infrastructure; drop it or move only reward-signal monitoring into dimension 1. Dimension 4, Deployment Hosting Strategy, is substantially out of scope because private-cloud hosting, distributed training (4.5), and compliance outcomes address general deployment infrastructure, not monitoring; drop it. Dimension 5 mixes relevant rollout controls with out-of-scope training and serving architecture; move validation-gated deployment, A/B testing, and rollback into dimension 6 and drop the remaining training/update values.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No dimension or value is an explicit catch-all bucket such as “Other,” “Miscellaneous,” or “Various techniques.” Broad options like 1.5 “Multi-layered evaluation signals” and 1.6 “Detector ensemble” describe specific combination strategies rather than serving as unspecified residual categories, so no catch-all reorganization is needed.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions combine multiple independent decisions rather than presenting one question with alternative answers. Split dimension 2, "Reward Integrity Strategy," into reward-objective representation (2.1–2.3, 2.6) and reward verification/enforcement (2.4–2.5, 2.7). Split dimension 5, "Policy Update and Release Strategy," into training/serving and update architecture (5.1–5.3, 5.5) and release, validation, and rollback (5.4, 5.6–5.8). Split dimension 6, "Incident Evidence and Containment," into detection/containment (6.1–6.4) and evidence, attribution, and learning (6.5–6.7). Dimension 7, "Feedback Data Collection Strategy," similarly mixes collection cadence/acquisition (7.1–7.4) with feedback reuse and supervision (7.5–7.6). Finally, dimension 1 mixes signal categories (1.1–1.4) with signal-combination strategies (1.5–1.6); split those into separate decisions. These reorganizations are needed for the post-deployment RL monitoring taxonomy to have one decision point per dimension.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: All seven dimensions have at least two non-outcome candidates, but several broad dimensions combine different decision questions. Split 1, "Monitoring Signal Selection," into signal types (1.1–1.4) and signal-combination/detector strategy (1.5–1.6). Split 2, "Reward Integrity Strategy," into reward representation (2.1–2.3, 2.6) and reward safeguards/verifier strategy (2.4–2.5, 2.7), leaving 2.8 as an outcome. Split 5, "Policy Update and Release Strategy," into update execution (5.1–5.3, 5.5) and release/rollback control (5.4, 5.6–5.8). Split 6, "Incident Evidence and Containment," into evidence and diagnosis (6.1, 6.5–6.7) and containment/traffic control (6.2–6.4). Split 7, "Feedback Data Collection Strategy," into collection cadence (7.1–7.2) and feedback construction/reuse (7.3–7.6). Dimension 4 also mixes hosting choices (4.1–4.4) with distributed training infrastructure (4.5), so 4.5 should be moved to an existing decision point whose question concerns training/compute infrastructure rather than being treated as a hosting alternative.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Statuses are generally valid and descriptions correctly frame accepted and rejected choices, such as 2.6 Single-metric optimization and 7.2 Single-batch feedback collection. However, 3.5 Behavior-only monitoring is labeled as an outcome even though its description is an alternative oversight strategy; relabel it as a rejected candidate decision or remove it from the outcome set. Also consolidate 2.1 Scalar proxy reward and 2.6 Single-metric optimization, which substantially duplicate the same reward-integrity alternative while carrying different statuses.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under at least one taxonomy dimension. Monitoring and drift choices in s19_p02, s08_p03, s02_p04, s17_p01, and s18_p03 map to Monitoring Signal Selection and Incident Evidence; reward design and hacking mitigation in s12_p03, s14_p04, s25_p13, s28_p05, and s06_p18 map to Reward Integrity Strategy; human oversight and explanation monitoring in s22_p07 and s27_p03 map to Oversight Allocation; deployment, A/B testing, rollback, and feedback-loop decisions in s07_p02, s20_p05, s21_p01, and s03_p03 map to Deployment, Release, Incident, and Feedback dimensions. The remaining passages are background or outcome-focused and do not require additional placement. No shortcoming identified.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers several major adopted options, including reward monitoring, structured rewards, hybrid verifiers, human oversight, A/B testing, safe fallback, and production experience pipelines. However, substantial options are unnamed: add BFAR, CUSUM, Hotelling, PSI/KL, and embedding-drift detection to dimension 1 (s02_p04, s08_p03); add gated reward accumulation, adversarial evaluation, policy/reward co-optimization, process-level consistency filtering, and the prevention methods listed in s06_p18 to dimension 2; add traffic shifting, version-pointer updates, and configuration-based rollback to dimension 6 (s07_p02); add API-gateway routing, rate limiting, authentication, edge deployment, and multi-model endpoints to dimension 4 (s21_p01, s20_p05); and add batch update cadence, ground-truth checks, and reset-to-saved-state recovery to dimensions 5 or 6 (s17_p01).

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have distinguishable questions, such as hosting (4), evidence collection (6), feedback acquisition (7), and reward verification (9). However, several pairs overlap. Update Execution Strategy (5) and Feedback Reuse Strategy (12) both cover ongoing adaptation and feedback-driven retraining; keep 5 for update timing and deployment coupling, and move reuse-specific values such as 12.1 Preference propagation and 12.2 Replay-buffer rehearsal exclusively under 12. Release and Rollback Strategy (10) and Incident Containment Strategy (11) duplicate staged rollout and fallback controls; move 11.1 Canary threshold control to 10 and retain 11 for incident-only containment. Monitoring Signal Types (1) and Monitoring Combination Strategy (8) overlap where 8.11 Internal interpretability audit and 8.9 LLM-based behavioral monitor answer what evidence is monitored rather than how signals are combined; move those values to 1. Reward Representation Strategy (2) and Feedback Acquisition Strategy (7) also overlap around human/preference reward inputs, especially 2.10 Human-approval reward signal and 7.4 Comparative preference supervision; keep the former as reward representation and the latter as feedback collection. These reorganizations would preserve distinct decision questions without merging dimensions that address different mechanisms.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions have recognizable decision topics and most values have informative descriptions, but substantial ambiguity remains. Dimension 1, "Monitoring Signal Types," contains overlapping values 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, and 1.7, especially the several Chain-of-Thought options; consolidate or rewrite them so evidence type, purpose, and combination are distinct. Dimension 2, "Reward Representation Strategy," has a description that does not cover its mixed values for representation, shaping, schedules, geometric proxies, and value learning; split the existing values into reward representation versus reward transformation/scheduling. Dimension 3 has near-duplicates such as 3.1 and 3.9, and 3.3 and 3.7; distinguish continuous oversight from event-triggered or risk-triggered review, or merge duplicates. Dimension 8 contains hard-to-separate monitoring alternatives, including 8.19-8.22 and 8.30, 8.31, and 8.44; define the monitored phenomenon and detection scope more explicitly or consolidate overlapping values. Dimension 9 duplicates adversarial testing in 9.8 and 9.19 and duplicates reward-hacking outcomes in 9.14 and 9.15; merge or sharpen these descriptions. Dimension 12 also has near-duplicates 12.2 and 12.13 concerning replay of historical and new data.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents the main decision areas for post-deployment RL monitoring with multiple alternatives in each: signal selection (1), monitoring combinations and detectors (8), oversight allocation (3), incident evidence (6), hosting and serving (4), updating (5), feedback acquisition and reuse (7, 12), reward verification (9), release and rollback (10), incident containment (11), and runtime intervention (13). Each of these dimensions contains several candidate values, such as detector ensembles versus rolling-window or tail monitoring in 8, human review versus automated review in 3, and canary, fallback, or ingestion-freeze controls in 11. No major monitoring-infrastructure area is represented only by a single candidate decision, so no reorganization is required under this criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains strong in-scope monitoring decisions, especially 1 Monitoring Signal Types, 3 Oversight Allocation Strategy, 6 Incident Evidence Strategy, 8 Monitoring Combination Strategy, 9 Reward Verification Strategy, and 11 Incident Containment Strategy. However, it substantially broadens beyond post-deployment monitoring infrastructure: (1) Reward Representation Strategy includes training and task-specific reward design such as 2.5-2.14; move only monitoring-relevant values into 8 or 9 and drop the remainder. (2) Deployment Hosting Strategy includes distributed training, privacy outcomes, and general API controls (4.5-4.11); retain monitoring-serving infrastructure and move incident controls to 6 or 11, dropping unrelated deployment values. (3) Update Execution Strategy is largely model-training and adaptation architecture (5.2-5.13, 5.16-5.18); move trigger-based retraining values 5.14-5.15 to 10 or 11 and drop the rest. (4) Feedback Acquisition Strategy and Feedback Reuse Strategy (7 and 12) focus on annotation, RLHF, and policy adaptation rather than monitoring; move production feedback collection to 6 and drop the remaining lifecycle/adaptation values. (5) Safe Action Intervention Strategy (13) mainly specifies runtime safety mechanisms; move monitoring-triggered intervention values 13.7 and 13.9 to 11 and drop the remaining action-policy design values.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Several broad catch-all buckets remain. Dimension 8, "Monitoring Combination Strategy," combines signal combination, granularity, cadence, automation, drift, novelty, performance, and evaluation methods; reorganize these existing values into narrower existing decision dimensions rather than using one umbrella bucket. Dimension 6, "Incident Evidence Strategy," similarly bundles collection, attribution, diagnosis, provenance, ingestion, and incident response; split or merge its values into more specific existing dimensions. Dimension 4, "Deployment Hosting Strategy," mixes hosting, streaming, API exposure, access control, and rate limiting; move the non-hosting values to the relevant operational or containment dimensions. Dimension 12, "Feedback Reuse Strategy," is a broad bucket spanning supervision, rehearsal, adaptation, evaluation, simulation, and enterprise integration; reorganize those values around the more specific feedback or update decisions. These broad descriptions make the taxonomy retain multiple 'various techniques' categories even though it has no literal 'Other' value.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are recognizable decisions for post-deployment RL monitoring, such as Monitoring Signal Types (1) and Oversight Allocation Strategy (3), but the taxonomy frequently bundles multiple decision points or makes implementation details into values. Monitoring Combination Strategy (8) combines signal selection, granularity, cadence, detector choice, drift evaluation, and alerting; split it into separate existing decision questions and assign the current values accordingly. Release and Rollback Strategy (10) combines release exposure with rollback triggers and recovery; split those into two dimensions using the existing values. Update Execution Strategy (5) similarly mixes training/serving placement, update timing, adaptation method, and retraining triggers; reorganize it into distinct decision questions. Deployment Hosting Strategy (4) contains serving-boundary controls such as API gateways, authentication, rate limiting, and stream processing (4.7-4.11), which are not hosting alternatives; move them into an appropriate existing operational-control dimension or split the dimension into hosting versus serving controls. Reward Representation Strategy (2) includes overly specific subtopics such as a red-block geometric proxy (2.9), reward schedules (2.8), and particular transformations/configurations (2.12-2.14); fold these into the descriptions of their broader existing alternatives rather than retaining them as standalone decision values.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The output contains many dimensions with at least two candidate decisions and correctly marks several effects as outcomes, but numerous broad dimensions combine decisions answering different questions. Most seriously, dimension 8, "Monitoring Combination Strategy," mixes signal composition (8.1-8.2), cadence and aggregation (8.3-8.8), anomaly and drift detection (8.9-8.24), KPI monitoring (8.25-8.34), and evaluation/testing methods (8.35-8.47); split these into separate decision points, keeping at least two candidates in each. Dimension 2, "Reward Representation Strategy," combines objective representation (2.1-2.4), reward transformations and schedules (2.5-2.8, 2.13), domain-specific reward examples and sources (2.9-2.12), and value-learning behavior (2.14); split or move those values to the decision points whose questions they answer. Dimensions 3, "Oversight Allocation Strategy," and 4, "Deployment Hosting Strategy," similarly mix allocation/timing/evidence choices and hosting/service/security controls; split each into coherent questions, with 4.10-4.11 forming a small but valid access-control decision. Dimensions 5, "Update Execution Strategy," 6, "Incident Evidence Strategy," and 7, "Feedback Acquisition Strategy" each combine multiple decision points such as update timing, update mechanism, retraining triggers, evidence collection, incident response, feedback cadence, and feedback source; split these clusters only where every resulting dimension retains at least two existing candidate values. Finally, dimensions 9, "Reward Verification Strategy," 10, "Release and Rollback Strategy," 12, "Feedback Reuse Strategy," and 13, "Safe Action Intervention Strategy" mix mechanisms with triggers, lifecycle choices, or outcomes; separate verification from testing, release from rollback triggers, feedback reuse from its effects, and runtime intervention from monitoring or learning choices.
